introduction.text: The Mausoleo Ossario Garibaldino on Rome’s Gianicolo hill is a monument that honors the soldiers who fought for the Roman Republic and later for the unification of Italy. It houses the remains of more than 1,600 patriots and serves as a national memorial to the struggle for freedom and national identity.

history.description: 1849: The last defense of the Roman Republic took place on the Gianicolo hill, marking the beginning of the period of battles that would last until 1870.
1849-1870: The period during which the Republic’s defenders and later patriots were killed in battles for Rome’s liberation.
1879: A law authorized the collection of the remains of those who died defending Rome, leading to the first provisional burial on the hill.
1884: Additional remains were interred in the mausoleum’s provisional burial area.
1941: The mausoleum was completed and inaugurated on 3 November, after two years of construction under the fascist regime.

design.description: The mausoleum features a quadriportico of travertine with three arches on each side, creating an open, columned façade.
At the center stands a single block of red granite from Baveno, forming the altar that bears allegorical Roman motifs.
Monolithic travertine pillars support bronze lion heads that are lit during official ceremonies.

art.description: Allegorical figures on the altar include the Capitoline wolf, the imperial eagle, and Roman legionary symbols, linking the 1849 Republic to ancient Rome.
Bronze lion heads and other decorative elements echo Roman iconography and reinforce the monument’s patriotic theme.
Mosaic ceilings and marble walls inside the crypt display votive palms, crosses, and inscriptions that honor the fallen.
